articles.title: Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us
articles.description: A TP-Link Wi-Fi 8 router. | Image: TP-Link TP-Link, one of the world's leading manufacturers of consumer Wi-Fi routers, is in a precarious position in the US. The company just launched its first Wi-Fi 8 routers, but can't bring them here because of President Donald Trump's foreign router ban. Even though competitors Netgear and Asus make their routers in Asia, they've mysteriously obtained blanket waivers for all their new gear; perhaps because of alleged ties to China, TP-Link hasn't managed to get such a waiver yet. articles.title: OPPO wins fast-charging injunctions in China as its 5G and VVC counteroffensive challenges ASUS’s licensing campaign

articles.title: The Workforce Behind the Roadmap
articles.description: For three years, every semiconductor conference has featured some version of the same slide: the industry doesn’t have enough people to build what it’s promising. This month, SEMI’s National Network for Microelectronics Education (NNME), backed by the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Commerce, named its first Industry Advisory Committee to turn those warnings into a national strategy, against a projected U.S. shortfall of 127,000 to 157,000 workers by 2030. The post The Workforce Behind the Roadmap appeared first on Semiconductor Digest.
